newsitem.title: PERU: Fujimori widens emergency rule in Peru.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori widens emergency rule in Peru.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori widened emergency rule in Peru on Friday as his "no concessions" stand on leftist rebels holding more than 100 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence won international backing.

A decree published in the official government gazette and signed by Fujimori said all of Lima and the neighbouring port of Callao had been placed under emergency rule, which gives the police and army greater powers, for 60 days.

Until Friday, a state of emergency imposed in the early 1980s to cope with guerrilla violence had covered only the centre and industrial outskirts of Lima and part of Peru's mountains and jungles. Fujimori decided to widen emergency powers a day after the Dec. 17 seizure of the residence by Marxist guerrillas of the Tupac Amaru movement demanding the release of jailed comrades.

The move took affect on Friday with its publication in El Peruano, the government gazette. A preamble said the decree had been issued to allow the government "to take corrective measures" in response to subversion.

Fujimori has flatly refused to give in to the rebels' demands and on Friday his stand won full support from Congress in a closed-door session called to discuss the hostage crisis. The government's refusal to negotiate the release of jailed guerrillas won backing on Friday from the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations and Russia.

In the toughest of a long stream of statements on the crisis from around the world, a G7 communique condemned the rebels as "terrorists" and promised to help the Peruvian government with "all the appropriate means that it could request."

Stressing the principle of no concessions to armed rebels, the communique issued in Paris coincided with reports that a U.S. spyplane had made high-altitude night flights over the residence and crack anti-terrorist units of the Peruvian police were training around a model of the building.
Earlier in the day, Japan, whose nationals account for the largest number of hostages after Peru, had called for unity in resolving the crisis.

"It is clear that the international community should not condone terrorism," Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda told a news conference. "It is also necessary ... to act as one to help resolve this crisis by setting free all the hostages peacefully, and at an early date."

The hardening position of the international community followed Christmas appeals from around the world, including Pope John Paul and U.S. President Bill Clinton. But the roughly 20 guerrillas holed up inside the booby-trapped residence showed no signs of changing their conditions for releasing hostages.

The guerrillas have released around 400 captives since storming the building. They have kept those they consider most useful as bargaining chips including two Peruvian ministers, Japanese businessmen, a handful of foreign diplomats and the brother of Fujimori.
They are demanding the release of around 400 jailed comrades in Peru, followed by safe passage to an Amazon jungle stronghold.

Peruvian intelligence sources told Reuters a U.S. spy plane had made several high-altitude night flights over the site of the siege, gathering information for a possible attack on guerrillas inside. They said the plane was a Schweitzer SA-2-37A equipped with infra-red cameras and used periodically in flights over drug-growing areas in the jungles of Peru, the world's largest producer of coca, the raw material for cocaine.
At the same time, police sources said crack troops had been training at a secret location outside Lima around a model of the residence in case the government ordered an assault.
Former hostages have warned against trying to overpower the guerrillas, who are armed with grenades, other explosives, AKM automatic rifles and ample ammunition.
Inside the residence, the hostages celebrated a birthday -- but it was not known whose. Journalists waiting outside the building heard a chorus of "Happy Birthday to You."

A former hostage, medical doctor Victor Lucero Rondon, said in a newspaper interview on Friday three of the captives were running serious health risks. But Red Cross members told a news conference their doctors were being allowed to take in medicines and treat hostages.
